content: Thomas Graham, a renowned chemist, was born on December 21, 1805, in Glasgow, Scotland. His father, a prosperous textile manufacturer, had aspirations for his son to join the Church of Scotland. However, Graham defied his father’s wishes and enrolled at the University of Glasgow in 1819. He graduated in 1826 and later became a professor of chemistry at several institutions, including the Royal College of Science and Technology and the University of London. In 1841, he founded the Chemical Society of London. His final professional role was as the Master of the Mint, a position he held for 15 years until his death on September 16, 1869. Notably, he was the last individual to hold this position. Thomas Graham is best known for two major scientific contributions. First, his research on the diffusion of gases led to the formulation of Graham's Law, which states that the rate of effusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass. Second, his pioneering work on colloids resulted in the discovery of dialysis. This breakthrough allowed him to separate colloids from crystalloids using a device called a dialyzer, which served as the precursor to modern dialysis machines. His studies in this area laid the foundation for the scientific discipline of colloid chemistry, a field in which Graham is recognized as the founder. Thomas Graham received numerous honors and accolades during his lifetime. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1836 and served as the first President of the Chemical Society of London in 1841. He was awarded the Royal Medal of the Royal Society twice, in 1837 and 1863, and received the prestigious Copley Medal in 1862. Additionally, he was honored with the Prix Jecker by the Paris Academy of Sciences in 1862. Posthumously, a statue of Graham was erected in Glasgow in 1872. The University of Strathclyde, where Graham worked at one of its predecessor institutions, named the building housing its chemistry department after him. Furthermore, the headquarters of the Royal Society of Chemistry in Cambridge, UK, is named the Thomas Graham House in his honor.
